background.definition: Charcot-Marie-Tooth (CMT) disease is a genetically heterogeneous group of disorders sharing the same clinical phenotype and affecting both motor and sensory nerves. CMT is characterized by distal limb muscle wasting and weakness (usually with skeletal deformities), distal sensory loss, and abnormalities of deep tendon reflexes.

list.listitem: CMT disease is the most common inherited neuromuscular disorder, with an estimated prevalence of 17 to 40 per 100,000 in the United States.
There are about 125,000 people with CMT in the United States.
A systematic review identified 12 studies of prevalence. It ranged from 9.7/100,000 persons in serbia to 82/100,000 persons in Norway. The percentage CMT1 vs CMT2 also varied by country.
Mutations of genes such as the myelin protein zero (MPZ) involved in different functions eventually lead to a length-dependent axonal degeneration.
Different mutations may result either in demyelinating CMT with slow conduction or in axonal CMT resulting in the distal predominance of the CMT phenotype.

The clinical phenotype is similar for CMT disease and is caused by mutations in many different genes involved in very diverse functions: coding for structural myelin proteins, gap-junction forming proteins, cytoskeleton elements, enzymes, and transcription factors.
Dysfunction of all these proteins, even when primarily affecting myelin, eventually leads to axonal degeneration that is length-dependent.
Patients with CMT usually present with progressive distal limb weakness, gait problems, muscle wasting, and bony deformities.
A family history of affected relatives is a key element in diagnosis.
Diagnostic testing is not always necessary, but EMG, nerve ultrasound, or biopsy and genetic testing may be considered when the diagnosis is in question. C

list.listitem: Ankle sprains, difficulty running, and falls are common early features. Ask about delayed developmental milestones, weakness, clumsiness, incoordination, fractures, and family history of affected relatives.
Loss of reflexes, pes cavus foot deformities, and hammer toes are the usual early physical changes.

Progression of the disease may lead to atrophy of muscles of the distal extremities, which in turn may cause gait disturbances, foot drop, weakness, clumsiness, and deformities ("stork leg" or inverted Champagne bottle changes in the distal upper and lower limbs).
Atrophic changes in the intrinsic muscles of the hands and feet and palpably enlarged peripheral nerves can be found. Distal extremities are usually most heavily involved.
Kyphosis and scoliosis can be a later development.
Hearing loss may occur due to involvement of cochlear nerves.
Vocal cord paresis is a rare complication that can cause speech difficulties.

Routine laboratory tests are normal in individuals with CMT disease. Genetic tests are available for some types of CMT disease. EMG can be used to refine the diagnosis and allow identification of subtypes of the disorder, but is often not definitive.
Ultrasonography of the median nerve and other peripheral nerves can assist in interpretation of EMG findings.
Histologic findings on nerve biopsy (usually the sural [short saphenous] nerve in the calf) include demyelination and axonal atrophy without inflammatory infiltrates.
Consider hip radiogrfaphs in all children to screen for hip dysplasia.
Suspect CMT in a patient with distal extremity muscle wasting, weakness, and a history of similarly affected family members.
Examine the patient for muscle atrophy in the distal extremities or intrinsic muscles of the hands and feet, loss of reflexes, and foot deformities (pes cavus, hammer toe).
EMG, nerve ultrasound, or nerve biopsy and genetic testing may be considered when the diagnosis is in question.
Treatment is largely supportive and adaptive.
There is no curative therapy; a therapeutic alliance is critical to support patients and families. C
Regular follow-up and therapeutic interventions, such as orthotics or physical or occupational therapy, are necessary to avoid joint contractures and deformities. C
Treat pain with medications, physical therapy and adaptive strategies. C

Surgery is sometimes necessary to correct deformities.
C
Medications might include analgesics for musculoskeletal pain, anticonvulsants or tricyclic antidepressants for neuropathic pain, and antispasmodics for muscle spasm.
Evidence-based guidelines found some support for use of gabapentin or pregabalin in patients with positive sensory symptoms.
It is better to manage chronic pain with regular dosing to achieve pain control.
Vincristine, isoniazid, paclitaxel, cisplatin, and nitrofurantoin are neurotoxic and should not be used in patients with CMT unless absolutely needed.
A 2022 evidence-based CMT guideline recommends against use of ascorbic acid, botulinum toxin, muscle relaxants or opioids.
Surgery is sometimes needed to correct deformities associated with soft tissue atrophy, contractures or bony changes stemming from these changes.
Cochlear implants may be considered for patients with significant hearing loss.

Evidence-based guidelines (2022) recommend referral to an orthopedic surgeon for children with painful, disabling or progressive pes cavus; ankle contractures; hip dysplasia; or moderate or worse scoliosis (Cobb ankle > 20 degrees).
There is no cure for CMT. Advances in genetics and molecular biology may eventually lead to effective prevention and treatment.

Adaptive, preventive and rehabilitative strategies include periodic monitoring, orthotics, orthopedic footwear, braces and regular stretching and aerobic exercises. Physical and occupational therapy as well as surgical treatments may be employed.

A Cochrane review concluded that strength training was beneficial in people with CMT, but that night splinting of the ankle(s) was ineffective. Overall, evidence was limited. A systematic review concluded that exercise to strengthen ankle dorsiflexors in children appears to be helpful.

Ankle dorsiflexion exercises for children are also recommended by a 2022 evidence-based CMT guideline. They also recommend a strength training program wit a focus on core muscles and a stretching program to avoid contractures. Ankle foot orthoses and balance training may be helpful in patients with foot drop, trips and falls, or instability.
Psychological support and an effective therapeutic alliance with the patient and family are important in such a chronic debilitating disease.

A systematic review of exercise for patients with CMT found only a few studies with small sample sizes, wide variation in interventions, and mixed quality. While some improvements in one or more measures were seen in most studies, the confidence in this evidence base is low and more research is needed.

A multidisciplinary approach including primary care coordination of a neurologist, surgeons, podiatrists, physiatrists, occupational and physical therapists, mental health and social service professionals is the optimal strategy.
Patients taking chemotherapy may experience severe neurotoxicity. This has been observed with vinca alkaloids, taxanes, and the combination of vinca alkaloids and platinum compounds.
The clinical course is extremely variable. Slow progression to atrophy, deformity, and decreased functional capacity is the usual course. C
CMT disease does not usually shorten the expected life span. B
Complications are increased in pregnancy because more interventions are needed to effect delivery.
Genetic counseling is important to allow families to make informed choices about childbearing.
Complications such as contractures, deformities, ulcerations, chronic pain syndromes, and depression can be reduced or prevented by regular monitoring.
